details:
**Things Fall Apart**
Achebe's first and most famous novel (1958), titled after a line in Yeats's "The Second Coming." It follows Okonkwo, a proud, hot-tempered leader of the Igbo village of Umuofia in what is now Nigeria, as his life and his society are torn apart by British colonialism and Christian missionaries. It is the first book of Achebe's "African Trilogy."

**Ikemefuna**
A boy from a neighboring village who is given to Umuofia as compensation for a murder and raised for three years in Okonkwo's household as a foster son. When the Oracle decrees that he must die, the elder Ezeudu warns Okonkwo not to take part. Okonkwo kills him anyway with his machete, so that he will not look weak.

**Ezeudu's son and the seven-year exile**
At Ezeudu's funeral, Okonkwo's gun accidentally explodes and kills Ezeudu's sixteen-year-old son. This is a "female" (accidental) crime, so Okonkwo and his family are exiled for seven years to Mbanta, his mother's homeland, and his compound is destroyed.

**Unoka, Amalinze the Cat, and the Week of Peace**
Okonkwo is ashamed of his lazy, debt-ridden, flute-playing father Unoka, and he wins fame as a young man by throwing the unbeaten wrestler Amalinze the Cat. He is punished for breaking the sacred Week of Peace by beating his wife Ojiugo. Another time he shoots at his wife Ekwefi after she cuts leaves from a banana tree.

**Nwoye becomes Isaac**
Okonkwo's sensitive eldest son Nwoye, who was deeply upset by Ikemefuna's death, is drawn to Christianity when missionaries arrive. When Okonkwo chokes him for it, Nwoye leaves home, converts, and takes the name Isaac. The missionaries include the gentle Mr. Brown, the zealous Mr. Smith, and the convert-leader Mr. Kiaga.

**Enoch unmasks an egwugwu**
In Things Fall Apart, the fanatical convert Enoch, also rumored to have killed and eaten the sacred python, tears the mask off an egwugwu (a masked ancestral spirit). In revenge, the villagers burn Mr. Smith's church. The District Commissioner tricks and jails Umuofia's leaders, including Okonkwo. Afterward Okonkwo beheads a court messenger and then hangs himself, and the Commissioner plans a book called The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger.

**The tortoise who called himself "All of You"**
A folktale told by Ekwefi to her daughter Ezinma in Things Fall Apart. The tortoise borrows feathers to go to a feast in the sky, renames himself "All of You" so that he gets all the food, and is punished when the angry birds take back their feathers. He falls and his shell shatters, which explains its cracked pattern.

**"An Image of Africa"**
Achebe's famous 1975 lecture, subtitled "Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness," which calls Joseph Conrad "a thoroughgoing racist" (originally "a bloody racist"). It argues that the novel presents Africa as "the other world," the antithesis of Europe, contrasting the "darkness" of the Congo with the Thames.

**No Longer at Ease**
Achebe's second novel (1960), titled from T. S. Eliot's "Journey of the Magi." Okonkwo's grandson Obi Okonkwo studies in England with money from the Umuofia Progressive Union, then joins the civil service in Lagos on a scholarship board. He wants to marry Clara Okeke, an osu (outcast), pays for her abortion, sinks into debt, and is arrested and tried for taking bribes.

**Arrow of God and Ezeulu**
Achebe's 1964 novel about Ezeulu, chief priest of the god Ulu in a group of Igbo villages called Umuaro. He refuses Captain Winterbottom's offer to make him a warrant chief for the colonial administration and is jailed, and he believes his priestly powers caused Winterbottom's illness.

**The Feast of the New Yam and John Goodcountry**
After his release, Ezeulu refuses to call the Feast of the New Yam until he has eaten the sacred yams he missed while in jail, so the harvest rots and famine looms. His son Obika dies while running in a funeral rite. The Christian catechist John Goodcountry offers protection to anyone who gives their harvest to the Christian god, and many villagers convert.

**A Man of the People**
Achebe's 1966 satire of postcolonial corruption, narrated by the young teacher Odili, who clashes with his former teacher Chief Nanga, the corrupt Minister of Culture. It ends with a military coup, and because a real coup happened in Nigeria just as it was published, Achebe was seen as a "prophet" and targeted by the military.

**Anthills of the Savannah**
Achebe's 1987 novel set in the fictional West African country of Kangan, ruled by the military dictator Sam, who wants to become President-for-Life. It follows his old school friends Chris Oriko, the Commissioner for Information, and Ikem Osodi, editor of the National Gazette, as well as Beatrice. It ends with a naming ceremony for a baby girl called Amaechina, "May-the-path-never-close."

**"Civil Peace"**
A short story set after the Nigerian Civil War. Jonathan Iwegbu is thankful to survive, runs a bicycle taxi, and receives twenty pounds as an "egg-rasher" (ex gratia payment) for turning in rebel money. When thieves rob him of it, he shrugs it off, saying "Nothing puzzles God."

**Other stories, poems, and nonfiction**
In "Dead Men's Path," the headmaster Michael Obi fences off a sacred ancestral path through his school, with disastrous results. In "Marriage Is a Private Affair," a father rejects his son's marriage until he learns he has grandsons. In "Vengeful Creditor," a young nursemaid feeds a baby red ink. Achebe also wrote the poem "Refugee Mother and Child" and the collection Beware, Soul Brother; children's books such as Chike and the River and How the Leopard Got His Claws; the essay collection Morning Yet on Creation Day; and the 2012 Biafran War memoir There Was a Country.
